query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Grain boundary oxidation and segregation governs degradation by promoting localized oxide formation that initiates microcracking, with intragranular oxidation playing a minor but measurable role.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built HEA with a fine-grained, homogeneous FCC matrix produced by additive manufacturing.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to elevated-temperature oxidizing conditions and compare them with samples that have been pre-annealed to achieve coarser grains.
generation.conditions: Temperatures between 750°C and 850°C in an oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., 10 mbar O2) for durations (e.g., 120 minutes) sufficient to induce surface oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries that act as fast diffusion channels where elemental segregation (particularly of Cr and Ti) leads to nucleation of brittle oxide phases, while intragranular regions experience slower, less concentrated oxidation.
generation.mechanism: The enhanced density of grain boundaries in fine-grained alloys accelerates elemental diffusion, causing preferential oxidation at these boundaries. This results in the formation of discontinuous, brittle oxide phases, which serve as crack initiation sites and compromise mechanical integrity, whereas intragranular oxidation remains at a lower rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Oxide formation will be concentrated along grain boundaries with observable microcracks; pre-annealed (coarser-grained) samples will display lower local oxidation rates and fewer microcracks. Intragranular oxidation is detectable but of lesser extent.
generation.baseline: Unexposed HEA with uniform, intact grain boundaries and minimal native oxide formation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is most active in materials with a high fraction of grain boundaries; in coarse-grained samples, grain-boundary effects diminish and intragranular oxidation may become relatively more significant.
generation.uncertainty: While grain-boundary effects are predicted to dominate, the quantitative contribution of intragranular oxidation remains to be precisely measured; however, existing evidence in similar alloys supports the primacy of boundary-mediated processes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one with fine grains (as additively manufactured) and another with coarsened grains via pre-annealing treatment. Expose both sets to identical oxidizing conditions and map oxide distribution using SEM/TEM with EDS, comparing grain boundaries and intragranular areas.
measurements: Grain size analysis by optical/SEM microscopy
Oxidation depth and spatial distribution via TEM/EDS mapping
Mechanical integrity assessments using nanoindentation or micro-cantilever tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If degradation (oxide formation and crack initiation) is not significantly more pronounced along grain boundaries than in intragranular regions, or if no differences are observed between fine-grained and coarse-grained samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Figure 4j summarizes these interactions where Mn-Al tends to have the strongest interaction and both Ni and Co being the weakest. This study uncovers the oxidation process in compositionally complex alloys. Our study involved subjecting an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy to oxidation at 400 °C under 10 mbar oxygen pressure for both ex situ and in situ observations. Ex situ observations, conducted using TEM after 120 min of oxidation, revealed a layered oxide structure. The 20 nm oxide layer on the equiatomic base alloy exhibited a composition sequence of Ni-rich (bottom layer), Cr-rich, and then Fe, Mn, and Co-rich layers (outer oxide).
